passages.label: A
passages.text: Look out of a high window in Milan's Vertical Forest and there may be a tree almost level with you. The project has two modern towers, one 110 metres high and the other 76 metres high, and people live in each apartment building. Both towers give plants an unusually large amount of space in a busy city.

passages.label: B
passages.text: The two towers carry about 800 trees, 4,500 shrubs and 20,000 other plants, and there are around 100 different plant species. Each home has its own mix, and the project page says every apartment has at least two trees, eight shrubs and forty plants. A small home and a large home both share the living green design.

passages.label: C
passages.text: The balconies extend about three metres from the towers. On each floor, trees and other plants sit between the glass windows and the city. An outer wall becomes the edge of a living green space. Someone in a small home may feel relaxed looking out at what seems like a private garden in the air.

passages.label: D
passages.text: Flying Gardeners use ropes to reach the plants outside, and the irrigation system needs regular inspection, and pruning requires tools that can stay secure in strong winds. The equipment and the safety of people below matter to the maintenance team. Inside, a room might have a chair, table and lamp next to the view. A sofa can make the space comfortable, and wooden or metal furniture may be chosen for the balcony. Looking out from a quiet room shows why plants near a window matter to people.

passages.label: E
passages.text: Solar panels on the roof supply some of the energy. The trees change colour and lose leaves at different times. In an old tower without places for trees outside each home, the windows would still have a city view of a different kind. These tall buildings show how well a new housing design can use the space outside its walls. From the street, someone can see why the two towers look different through the year. Each living group of plants belongs to part of a home.

passages.label: A
passages.text: In Schijndel, a big farm house seems to stand in the market square. The image can be seen across the square, but behind it is a public building with a modern use. The Dutch architects MVRDV designed Glass Farm to fill a space that had remained open for many years after the old buildings were lost.

passages.label: B
passages.text: The architects wanted the form to connect with local history. They photographed the remaining old farms around the town. Artist Frank van der Salm photographed the historic farms for the project. With the architects, he combined details from these buildings into one large image of a typical traditional farmhouse, and the image did not copy one real farm. It represented shared parts of many farms from the area, and the combined picture shows details that people in the town know well. The big outline helps visitors see those details while they walk toward the square or stand some way back.

passages.label: C
passages.text: The glass outside wall carries a printed picture of a traditional farm, and the building is about fourteen metres high. Its roof shape and tall picture of a door have been made bigger than the ordinary objects they show. Near the main entrance the image of the door is about four metres high.

passages.label: D
passages.text: Daylight passes through pale parts of the picture and goes through the printed glass at different levels. Inside, a room may contain a chair, table or lamp like an ordinary café, and a wooden surface is easy to imagine when looking at the image. The wood in the picture and the hard glass show why someone near the building has a different view from someone across the square.

passages.label: E
passages.text: People enter shops and places to eat, and the ground floor helps connect the building to the life of the square. A new material makes an old roof shape and a farm image part of the place where people go today. Visitors under the high ceiling may find the inside comfortable and quiet. A metal fitting or a desk in a shop can give away the modern use of the place.

passages.label: A
passages.text: Jewel Changi Airport stands beside the passenger terminal area in Singapore. A big round building with a glass roof brings travel services, shops and nature together. It is possible to meet someone, walk in a garden or stop to eat before going to the areas used for flights. A person with time before a flight can find a place to sit. Nearby residents can use the same spaces without taking a flight.

passages.label: B
passages.text: At the centre is the Rain Vortex. Water falls from a high point forty metres to the basement, passing through seven storeys. In the day, visitors can watch from a path. In the evening, light changes the view, and a beautiful waterfall is the first thing many people see in this modern part of the airport.

passages.label: C
passages.text: The Forest Valley surrounds the waterfall. And it has more than 900 trees and palms and approximately 60,000 shrubs. Paths cross the indoor garden on several levels, and one walk takes about thirty minutes. Seats and exits along the way allow visitors to stop or leave, so they can choose a comfortable pace and feel relaxed.

passages.label: D
passages.text: Passengers can take a lift or use stairs between several levels of the Forest Valley, where the entrance and exit are integrated into pedestrian routes. A chair or table in a quiet area gives travellers a comfortable place to look up at the ceiling. Vegetation, circulation and the sound of falling water distinguish this sheltered space from a noisy airport terminal.

passages.label: E
passages.text: Canopy Park sits high above the entrance floor, and there are gardens, paths, places to eat and space for children to play. A tall indoor space makes room for small stops as well as longer walks. The shopping centre below the park gives people another place to go before they return to the passenger area. Canopy Park covers approximately 14,000 square metres, giving visitors a different perspective on the layout of this airport building. A room near the garden gives a different perspective on the roof and the interior planting.

questions.instruction: Choose ONE answer, A–D, for each question.
questions.prompt: What shows that the building has a wider purpose than serving people about to board a plane?
options: Everyone inside the building is waiting to take a flight.
Each visitor has to walk through the garden before checking in.
People who live nearby can use the same spaces without flying.
Every shop is described as being inside an aircraft.

questions.instruction: Choose ONE answer, A–D, for each question.
questions.prompt: What stays the same and what changes between daytime and evening in the account of the centre?
options: It is the same waterfall, but evening light changes how it looks.
At night the waterfall is moved from the basement to the roof.
The waterfall is only in the building in the evening.
The water stops passing through the building whenever daylight changes.

questions.instruction: Choose ONE answer, A–D, for each question.
questions.prompt: Why could a half-hour route suit a visitor who does not want to finish it in one go?
options: The walker must stay on the path until reaching its only exit.
The full walk replaces the trip to the passenger area.
Visitors can leave by any shop window halfway along the route.
The route offers places to sit or ways to leave while exploring.

questions.instruction: Choose ONE answer, A–D, for each question.
questions.prompt: Which pair describes a way to watch the waterfall and a way to shorten a walk near it?
options: The area stays empty during daylight, so neither activity depends on a place to watch.
A path gives a view of the falling water, and seats or exits let people shorten or break up a walk.
The waterfall stops on each level so that all walks have the same length.
Lights in the evening show that visitors must finish the longest route.

questions.instruction: Choose ONE answer, A–D, for each question.
questions.prompt: What makes the indoor area feel different from a noisy passenger terminal?
options: People can hear falling water and spend time among plants.
People have to stay next to the loudest busy area.
Every room has the same lighting and seating as a departure gate.
The path is used only to carry bags from the terminal.

questions.instruction: Choose ONE answer, A–D, for each question.
questions.prompt: A passenger wants to change levels without using steps and then pause somewhere quiet. Which plan fits?
options: Use only the stairs and stand while watching the departure gate.
Take the waterfall path down to the basement, where every visitor has to stop.
Use the lift to change levels and find a seat in a quiet area.
Stay at the entrance because no other level has anywhere to sit.

questions.instruction: Choose ONE answer, A–D, for each question.
questions.prompt: What further choice does the description of the high park add for a person near the passenger area?
options: It is the only place where a passenger is allowed to wait.
It gives different things to do above shopping areas before returning to the passenger space.
It is a long outdoor route with no places to stop.
It removes the need for aircraft at the airport.

questions.instruction: Choose ONE answer, A–D, for each question.
questions.prompt: Which explanation accounts for both a long view through the building and a choice of different levels from which to explore?
options: The floor and roof lie at the same height and there are no levels in between.
Only the entrance level is used and the water stays on that level.
The shopping area takes up the whole building so no levels can be connected.
Water falls through several storeys, and visitors can reach different levels by paths, stairs or lift.

questions.instruction: Choose ONE answer, A–D, for each question.
questions.prompt: A traveller only has a short time and a local visitor wants a longer outing. Which plan fits the available things to do?
options: One can stop to sit or eat, while the other takes time for a garden walk.
Both must follow the same long route and leave at the same time.
The traveller must go straight through the park and the local visitor must leave without entering.
Only the traveller is allowed to stay in the building for a while.

questions.instruction: Choose ONE answer, A–D, for each question.
questions.prompt: Which idea is supported by the article as a whole?
options: All the plants are on the outside of the airport and only passengers can see them.
The building uses its height only for transporting people to shops.
It combines travel with a range of ways to spend time in a planted building on several levels.
The building has one route with no distinction between viewing, shopping and travel.
